articles.title: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.
articles.content:
Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%

The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."

A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors

The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."

The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in quantum computing by overcoming a major obstacle to scaling silicon spin qubits with high accuracy. This advancement has broad implications for the future of powerful, fault-tolerant quantum computers, which could revolutionize computing technology and benefit society at large. The article provides detailed context about the problem, the solution, and its impact, fulfilling criteria for inspiring good news.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden flaw that challenges 40 years of superconductor science
articles.summary: A superconducting material studied for 40 years has turned out to be far more complex than scientists believed. Advanced 3D imaging revealed a hidden patchwork of crystal structures, with unusually wide boundaries that may weaken superconductivity. The discovery challenges decades of scientific assumptions and could explain why some superconductors outperform others.
articles.content:
Scientists at the University of Warwick have uncovered a surprising secret inside a superconductor that researchers have studied for 40 years. Long believed to have a uniform crystal structure, the material actually contains a complex patchwork of different atomic arrangements. Using an advanced 3D imaging technique, the team was able to see deep inside the crystal for the first time, revealing hidden features that challenge decades of scientific assumptions.

High-temperature superconductivity ranks among the most important scientific breakthroughs of the past four decades. Superconductors can carry electrical current without any resistance, eliminating the energy losses that normally occur as electricity travels through conventional materials. They also have the potential to support extraordinarily powerful magnets, making them promising for future power grids, medical scanners, and quantum computers.

The new findings, published in Physical Review Letters, come from researchers in Warwick's Department of Chemistry working with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in France. Their investigation focused on a class of copper-based superconductors known as cuprates, which can conduct electricity without resistance at unusually high (though still very cold) temperatures.

Advanced 3D Imaging Reveals a Hidden Crystal Structure

For four decades, scientists have generally built their theories of cuprate superconductivity around the assumption that these materials have the same crystal structure throughout their interiors. The new research shows that this fundamental assumption does not always hold.

To investigate, the team used scanning 3D X-ray diffraction, a sophisticated imaging method that reveals how atoms are arranged deep within a crystal. The approach is similar in principle to a medical CT scan, except that it maps atomic structures rather than tissues and organs.

This allowed the researchers to construct a detailed three-dimensional picture of the superconductor's interior, exposing structural variations that conventional techniques had not revealed.

Instead of finding a uniform crystal, they discovered a patchwork of regions containing two slightly different atomic arrangements. Even more surprising were the boundaries separating these regions, which were hundreds of times wider than expected.

These unusually broad transition zones were not simply narrow dividing lines between neighboring structures. They were extensive enough to behave almost like distinct structures themselves, potentially influencing how electricity moves through the material.

A 40-Year Assumption About Superconductors Overturned

Professor Mark Senn, who led the study at the University of Warwick's Department of Chemistry, explained why the findings could have major implications for superconductivity research.

"For forty years, the working assumption has been that these materials are the same all the way through, and nearly all the theory is built on that picture. We've shown it doesn't hold. The crystal is fundamentally patchworked and textured, with unusually wide boundary regions that likely work against superconductivity rather than just sitting alongside it.

"This might explain why some materials perform better than others and means some existing bulk measurements will need to be reinterpreted and future theoretical models built that incorporate this structural complexity."

The discovery suggests that the internal boundaries may actively interfere with superconductivity rather than simply coexist with it. If that is the case, the hidden structural differences could help explain why certain superconducting materials perform better than others.

It also means that some previous experiments, particularly those measuring the overall properties of these materials, may need to be reconsidered. Future theories will likely need to account for the complex structures inside real crystals rather than treating them as perfectly uniform.

What the Discovery Means for Future Superconductors

The researchers suspect that similar hidden structural patterns may be widespread among other cuprate superconductors. They could also occur in related materials being investigated for their ability to become superconducting under extreme pressure.

Beyond challenging existing theories, the study demonstrates the power of a new generation of imaging technology.

The advanced measurements were made possible by a recent 150 million euro upgrade to the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, which provides extremely intense X-ray beams for studying materials in extraordinary detail.

This technology now allows scientists to examine the three-dimensional interiors of many different materials with a level of precision that was previously unavailable. By revealing how hidden atomic structures affect a material's behavior, the technique could provide valuable insights across materials science.

For superconductivity research, the implications are particularly important. Understanding how internal crystal structures influence electrical performance could eventually help scientists identify ways to improve superconducting materials, bringing more advanced energy systems, powerful magnets, medical imaging devices, and quantum technologies closer to reality.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery that challenges long-standing assumptions about superconductors, revealing complex internal structures that impact their performance. This breakthrough has broad implications for improving superconducting materials, which are crucial for energy efficiency, medical technology, and quantum computing, thus offering meaningful benefits to society.

articles.title: From agriculture to AI-griculture: How tech is changing farming
articles.summary: From remote monitoring of cattle to automation of processes that took up valuable time, farmers in NI are rapidly becoming skilled in technology.
articles.content:
George McMaster's farming career started with milking eight cows in a byre, relying on his eyes to spot any health issues in his cattle.

He still watches his now-300-strong herd, but via a feed from an AI camera in the milking parlour at the farm near Islandmagee in County Antrim.

The device uses an algorithm which assigns each cow its own ID, records a short video of the animal every day, analyses it and flags any changes - often before they are visible to the human eye.

For the third generation farmer, it is "absolutely incredible to move from all hand-done to sitting on the phone, watching what's happening outside".
articles.reasoning: The article describes a meaningful technological advancement in agriculture where AI is used to monitor cattle health more efficiently and proactively, benefiting farmers and potentially improving animal welfare. The impact is broad as it represents a significant shift in farming practices with tangible benefits.

articles.title: New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
articles.summary: Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic. Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land.
articles.content:
For millions of years, evolution helped animals make the transition from life in the ocean to life on land. But the journey did not always move in one direction. Many species eventually returned to the water, developing new adaptations that allowed them to thrive in aquatic environments.

Dozens of major groups of mammals and reptiles made this remarkable evolutionary reversal. Now, a new study from Yale University is shedding light on when and how these transitions occurred, as well as which ancient animals became fully aquatic and which continued to depend on land.

The findings were published in the journal Current Biology.

"These secondarily aquatic groups adapted in strikingly similar ways to their new aquatic home -- evolving flippers and a suite of other features that made them better swimmers," said lead author Caleb Gordon, who completed his doctorate at Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences (GSAS) earlier this year and is now a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum of Natural History. "As a result, they've become textbook examples of convergent evolution, which can tell us a lot about the processes driving and constraining adaptive change in response to similar environmental cues."

Using Ancient Fossils and AI to Reconstruct Evolution

To investigate these evolutionary changes, the researchers examined hundreds of fossil and modern specimens housed at the Yale Peabody Museum and dozens of other institutions worldwide. They collected extensive new data, including measurements (more than 11,000), photographs, and CT scans.

The team combined traditional paleontological techniques with machine learning models that account for evolutionary relationships. They also incorporated a statistical approach originally used by naval forces during World War II. Together, these methods offered a new way to investigate one of the most remarkable transitions in vertebrate evolution.

"Reconstructing the lives of extinct life forms in a scientifically rigorous way, as opposed to just telling stories, is a precise and delicate undertaking," said Bhart-Anjan Bhullar, senior author of the study. Bhullar is an associate professor of Earth and planetary sciences in Yale's Faculty of Arts and Sciences (FAS) and an associate curator of vertebrate paleontology and vertebrate zoology at the Peabody Museum.

"It requires a careful interweaving of data from modern organisms, of which our understanding is necessarily far deeper, and knowledge of these living organisms' genealogy relative to fossil forms," he said. "Caleb's work accomplishes all of this and more, and on a massive evolutionary scale."

For decades, scientists have disagreed about when particular groups of prehistoric animals became fully adapted to life underwater. The fossil record often provides incomplete or conflicting clues, making it difficult to determine whether an extinct species primarily lived on land, in water, or in both environments.

Some skeletal features may indicate an aquatic lifestyle, while others suggest that the same animal remained capable of moving and feeding on land. These contradictions have led researchers to different conclusions about how ancient species behaved.

"In these cases, paleontologists are often stuck, as different lines of evidence disagree about what the ancient animal was like," Gordon said.

To address this uncertainty, Gordon developed a method using relatively simple but effective machine learning models trained on living animals. By identifying relationships between skeletal proportions and known lifestyles, the models can estimate how extinct species used aquatic environments. They can also predict soft tissue adaptations, including swimming structures that rarely survive in fossils.

Spinosaurus May Have Spent Most of Its Life Underwater

One of the most striking findings concerns Spinosaurus, a giant prehistoric dinosaur whose relationship with water has generated considerable controversy.

Spinosaurus lived approximately 113 million to 94 million years ago in what is now northern Africa. Although scientists generally agree that it was associated with aquatic environments, exactly how it moved, hunted, and spent its time remains a subject of debate.

Some evidence points to an animal that frequently submerged itself and pursued prey underwater, much like seals or penguins. Other findings suggest a lifestyle closer to that of a modern heron, with Spinosaurus walking and searching for food along shorelines and in shallow water.

The Yale team's analysis provides new support for the more aquatic interpretation.

"Our results shed new light on how much time Spinosaurus spent submerged, which could support the underwater hunting view," Gordon said. "We confidently recovered highly aquatic habits for Spinosaurus, indicating that it spent the vast majority of its time submerged in the water."

Although the findings do not settle every question about how Spinosaurus hunted, they strengthen the case that this enormous predator spent much more of its life underwater than on land.

Ancient Marine Reptiles That Never Fully Left Land

The researchers reached a different conclusion about mesosaurs, small marine reptiles that lived between 290 million and 274 million years ago in regions now forming parts of South Africa and eastern South America.

Mesosaurs have long interested paleontologists because they gave birth to live young, a characteristic some researchers have interpreted as evidence of a fully aquatic existence. However, the new analysis suggests that their limbs were not adapted for a life spent entirely in water.

Instead, their skeletal proportions indicate that mesosaurs regularly moved between aquatic and terrestrial environments.

"They spent a lot of time on land, like a modern-day alligator or platypus does," Gordon said. "Mesosaurs didn't completely leave the land behind."

The findings also suggest a broader pattern among the earliest marine reptiles. According to the researchers, all Paleozoic marine reptiles (all marine reptiles around before the dinosaurs appeared) continued to return to land regularly. None appeared to have evolved a completely aquatic lifestyle, with even the most water adapted species remaining amphibious.

The researchers found that forelimb proportions were particularly useful for distinguishing these lifestyles. Using this information, their models could predict with more than 90% accuracy whether an animal possessed soft tissue flippers and whether it had highly or fully aquatic habits.

A World War II Technique Helps Solve an Evolutionary Mystery

An especially unusual part of the research involved adapting a statistical method developed during the 1940s.

"Caleb resurrected a statistical technique from a bygone era," said co-author Jacques Gauthier, a professor of Earth and planetary sciences at Yale and curator-in-charge for vertebrate paleontology at the Peabody Museum. "It was developed during WWII to estimate the probability that an approaching blip on the radar screen was an enemy plane. Caleb cleverly used it to get at whether or not an extinct animal had limbs modified for swimming."

By repurposing this approach, the researchers could assess the likelihood that an extinct species possessed specialized swimming adaptations, even when direct evidence of those features was missing.

The method could eventually help scientists investigate other major changes in evolutionary history. Potential applications include studying when human ancestors developed the ability to walk on two legs and how the dinosaur ancestors of birds evolved the ability to fly.

A New Way to Understand Extinct Animals

Because most prehistoric vertebrates are known primarily through their fossilized skeletons, reconstructing their behavior is one of paleontology's greatest challenges. Bones preserve valuable information, but they rarely provide a complete picture of how an animal lived.

Traditionally, scientists have interpreted particular skeletal features to make arguments about the lifestyles of extinct species. Those interpretations can differ significantly, especially when fossils are incomplete or several anatomical characteristics point toward different conclusions.

The new approach offers a more systematic way to evaluate that evidence, using patterns observed in living species to make testable predictions about animals that disappeared millions of years ago.

"Bones are all that is left to us of the vast majority of vertebrate animals that have lived on Earth," Bhullar said. "We want to know so very much about these creatures and the succession of lost worlds they inhabited, but we have so little on which to base our conclusions. From skeletal remains, people have tried to discern life habits, generally making an argument on the basis of one preferred set of features or another. Caleb's method removes the subjectivity from this process and allows the data to speak for themselves."

The study's additional co-authors are Lisa Freisem, a doctoral student at Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, and Christopher Griffin, an assistant professor of geosciences at Princeton University who previously worked as a postdoctoral fellow at Yale.

Research support was provided by the Yale Institute for Biospheric Studies, the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Crocodile Specialist Group, and the National Science Foundation.

articles.personality_title: New study reveals Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Millions of years ago, some animals that had moved from water to land went back to living in water. Scientists have long debated which prehistoric creatures were fully aquatic and which still spent time on land.

**What happened** – Researchers at Yale University used machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements to study ancient animals' lifestyles. Their new method combined fossil data with modern animal studies and a World War II statistical technique. They discovered that Spinosaurus, a large dinosaur from northern Africa, likely spent the majority of its life submerged underwater. In contrast, smaller marine reptiles called mesosaurs still spent much time on land.

**Impact** – This research provides clearer evidence about how extinct animals lived, solving long-standing debates. It shows that Spinosaurus was more aquatic than previously thought, while some ancient reptiles considered fully aquatic were actually amphibious. The use of machine learning and old statistical methods offers a new, more reliable way to study fossils and understand ancient life.

**What's next step** – The team’s method can be used to study other extinct animals and major evolutionary changes, such as how early humans began walking upright or how dinosaurs evolved into birds. This approach may help scientists uncover more details about the lives of creatures from the past.

**One-sentence takeaway** – By combining fossils with machine learning, scientists have found strong evidence that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient reptiles remained partly land-dwelling.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle étude révèle que le Spinosaurus passait la plupart de sa vie sous l'eau
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Il y a des millions d'années, certains animaux qui étaient passés de l'eau à la terre sont retournés vivre dans l'eau. Les scientifiques débattaient depuis longtemps pour savoir quelles créatures préhistoriques étaient entièrement aquatiques et lesquelles passaient encore du temps sur la terre ferme.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs de l'université de Yale ont utilisé l'apprentissage automatique et des milliers de mesures de fossiles pour étudier le mode de vie des animaux anciens. Leur nouvelle méthode a combiné des données fossiles avec l'étude d'animaux modernes et une technique statistique de la Seconde Guerre mondiale. Ils ont découvert que le Spinosaurus, un grand dinosaure d'Afrique du Nord, passait probablement la majorité de sa vie immergé sous l'eau. En revanche, de petits reptiles marins appelés mésosaures passaient encore beaucoup de temps sur la terre.

**Impact** – Cette recherche apporte des preuves plus claires sur la façon dont vivaient les animaux éteints, résolvant des débats anciens. Elle montre que le Spinosaurus était plus aquatique qu'on ne le pensait, tandis que certains reptiles anciens considérés comme entièrement aquatiques étaient en fait amphibies. L'utilisation de l'apprentissage automatique et de méthodes statistiques anciennes offre une nouvelle façon plus fiable d'étudier les fossiles et de comprendre la vie ancienne.

**Prochaine étape** – La méthode de l'équipe peut être utilisée pour étudier d'autres animaux éteints et des changements évolutifs majeurs, comme la façon dont les premiers humains ont commencé à marcher debout ou comment les dinosaures ont évolué en oiseaux. Cette approche pourrait aider les scientifiques à découvrir plus de détails sur la vie des créatures du passé.

**Une phrase clé** – En combinant fossiles et apprentissage automatique, les scientifiques ont trouvé de solides preuves que le Spinosaurus passait la majeure partie de sa vie sous l'eau, tandis que certains reptiles anciens restaient partiellement terrestres.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo estudio revela que el Spinosaurus pasó la mayor parte de su vida bajo el agua
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Hace millones de años, algunos animales que habían pasado del agua a la tierra volvieron a vivir en el agua. Los científicos han debatido durante mucho tiempo cuáles criaturas prehistóricas eran completamente acuáticas y cuáles aún pasaban tiempo en tierra.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Yale usaron aprendizaje automático y miles de mediciones de fósiles para estudiar el estilo de vida de animales antiguos. Su nuevo método combinó datos fósiles con estudios de animales modernos y una técnica estadística de la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Descubrieron que el Spinosaurus, un gran dinosaurio del norte de África, probablemente pasó la mayor parte de su vida sumergido bajo el agua. En cambio, pequeños reptiles marinos llamados mesozoos todavía pasaban mucho tiempo en tierra.

**Impacto** – Esta investigación ofrece evidencia más clara sobre cómo vivían los animales extintos, resolviendo debates antiguos. Muestra que el Spinosaurus era más acuático de lo que se pensaba, mientras que algunos reptiles antiguos considerados completamente acuáticos eran en realidad anfibios. El uso del aprendizaje automático y métodos estadísticos antiguos ofrece una forma nueva y más confiable de estudiar fósiles y entender la vida antigua.

**Próximo paso** – El método del equipo puede usarse para estudiar otros animales extintos y grandes cambios evolutivos, como cómo los primeros humanos empezaron a caminar erguidos o cómo los dinosaurios evolucionaron a aves. Este enfoque puede ayudar a los científicos a descubrir más detalles sobre la vida de criaturas del pasado.

**Una frase clave** – Al combinar fósiles con aprendizaje automático, los científicos encontraron evidencia sólida de que el Spinosaurus pasó la mayor parte de su vida bajo el agua, mientras que algunos reptiles antiguos seguían siendo parcialmente terrestres.
